questions.stem:
Consider the digital circuit shown below with two input lines A and B, two select lines S0 and S1, and an output line Y. The blocks Q and M represent active high 2:4 decoder and 4-to-1 multiplexer, respectively. Out of 16 possible input combinations, the number of combinations that produce $Y=1$ is ____________. (answer in integer)

Note: One input combination is an instance of [A B S1 S0].
questions.figure: Decoder Q has inputs A and B and outputs D0, D1, D2, D3. Multiplexer M has data inputs 0, 1, 2, 3 and select lines S1, S0, with output Y. D0 is wired to M input 0, the constant 0 to input 1, the constant 1 to input 2, and D3 to input 3. D1 and D2 are not connected.

diagram.alt: Decoder Q with inputs A, B and outputs D0 to D3 feeds multiplexer M: D0 goes to input 0, constant 0 to input 1, constant 1 to input 2, D3 to input 3; selects S1 S0, output Y.

solutionDiagram.alt: Table for each A B pair showing D0, D3, the four multiplexer inputs, the output Y for each select value, and the count of ones: 2, 1, 1, 2, total 6.

steps.title: The two parts and the one rule for each
steps.body: A decoder with $n$ inputs has $2^n$ outputs and exactly one of them is 1 at any time: the output whose number equals the binary value of the inputs. Here "active high" means the chosen output is 1 and the others are 0. So for the 2:4 decoder, $D_i = 1$ only when $AB$ read as a binary number equals $i$. A multiplexer (MUX) is a data selector: with select lines $S_1S_0$ read as a binary number $s$, its output $Y$ equals the data input numbered $s$. The question counts input combinations $[A\,B\,S_1\,S_0]$ (16 of them) for which $Y = 1$.

steps.title: Write the four MUX inputs in terms of A and B
steps.body: From the figure the data inputs are: input 0 = $D_0$, input 1 = constant 0, input 2 = constant 1, input 3 = $D_3$. Since $D_0 = 1$ only for $AB = 00$ and $D_3 = 1$ only for $AB = 11$, we get $D_0=\overline{A}\,\overline{B}$ and $D_3 = AB$.

steps.title: Count by select value
steps.body: Take each value of $S_1S_0$ and ask for how many of the four $AB$ pairs $Y=1$. Select 00: $Y=D_0$, which is 1 for one pair ($AB=00$). Select 01: $Y=0$ for every pair, so 0 pairs. Select 10: $Y=1$ for every pair, so 4 pairs. Select 11: $Y=D_3$, which is 1 for one pair ($AB=11$).

steps.title: Add up
steps.body: $1 + 0 + 4 + 1 = 6$ combinations give $Y=1$. The worked table gives the same total when counted by rows of $AB$: $2+1+1+2=6$. The answer is 6, matching the official key.

shortcut.body: Count by select value. A constant 1 on a data input gives 4 combinations (all four $AB$ pairs), a constant 0 gives none, and a decoder output $D_i$ is 1 for exactly one $AB$ pair, giving 1 combination. Inputs are $D_0, 0, 1, D_3$, so the total is $1+0+4+1=6$. The shortcut is safe whenever each data input is a constant or a single decoder output.

traps.text: Counting only the two decoder inputs that are wired, or forgetting that the constant 1 on input 2 makes $Y=1$ for all four $AB$ pairs: that gives 2, not 6.

Counting 8: treating the constants as one combination each instead of four, or taking all of $S_1S_0=10$ and $S_1S_0=11$ rows. A constant is true for every value of the other variables, so it contributes 4.
Thinking decoder outputs D1 and D2 matter. They are unconnected, so they play no part, and answering 5 by leaving out one of the decoder terms is the usual slip.

recognize.clues: The stem names an active high 2:4 decoder whose outputs feed a 4-to-1 multiplexer, and it counts input combinations of [A B S1 S0] with Y=1. Each decoder output is 1 for exactly one (A, B) pair.
recognize.contrast: A multiplexer-only question gives data inputs that are free variables, so an input can be 1 for half the cases. Here a data input from the decoder is 1 for one pair in four, and a constant 1 is 1 for all four.

check.body: Count by rows of $AB$ instead. $AB=00$ makes $D_0=1$, so $Y=1$ at $S_1S_0=00$ and at $10$. $AB=01$ and $AB=10$ make $D_0$ and $D_3$ both 0, so only $S_1S_0=10$ works. $AB=11$ makes $D_3=1$, so $S_1S_0=10$ and $11$ work. The four rows contribute 2, 1, 1, 2 and the sum matches the count by select value.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2026 Set 2, Question 49
GATE 2026 CS-2 answer key, IIT Guwahati

hints.text: Each of the 16 combinations of A, B, S1 and S0 gives one value of Y. Which part of the circuit decides Y once S1 and S0 are fixed, and which inputs does that part still depend on?
An active high 2:4 decoder drives exactly one of its four outputs to 1 for each value of its two inputs. A multiplexer copies the data input whose number is given by its select lines.
Fix the select lines first. Then Y is a single data input, and the task is to count the (A, B) pairs for which that wire is 1. A constant wire has the same value for every (A, B) pair.
Make a table with one row for each value of S1S0. In each row write which wire is copied to Y and when that wire is 1 in terms of A and B. Decoder outputs that are not wired do not appear.
Take the row S1S0 = 01: the wire copied there is the constant 0, so no (A, B) pair gives 1 in that row. Do the other three rows the same way and add the four counts.

variation.stem: A 2:4 active high decoder with inputs A and B (outputs D0 to D3) feeds a 4-to-1 multiplexer with select lines S1 and S0. The multiplexer data inputs 0, 1, 2, 3 are wired to D1, the constant 1, the constant 1 and D2, in that order. How many of the 16 combinations of [A B S1 S0] give $Y=1$? (answer in integer)
variation.explanation: Count by select value. Input 0 is $D_1$, which is 1 for one $AB$ pair, giving 1. Inputs 1 and 2 are the constant 1, each giving 4. Input 3 is $D_2$, giving 1. The total is $1+4+4+1=10$.

questions.stem:
Consider the following logic circuit diagram.

Which is/are the CORRECT option(s) for the output function $F$?
questions.figure: Inputs Y and X. Gate 1 is a NAND with inputs Y and X. Gate 2 is a NOT with input X. Gate 3 is an AND with inputs X and NOT Y (Y passes through a NOT first). The outputs of Gate 1, Gate 2 and Gate 3 all feed one OR gate whose output is F.

diagram.alt: Three gates in parallel feeding an OR gate: NAND of Y and X, NOT of X, and AND of X with NOT Y; the OR output is F.

solutionDiagram.alt: Truth table for X Y over four rows listing the three gate outputs, F, and the value of each of the four options; options A, B and C match F in every row, D does not.

options: $\overline{XY}$
$\overline{X} + \overline{Y} + X\overline{Y}$
$\overline{XY} + \overline{X} + X\overline{Y}$
$X + \overline{Y}$

steps.title: What a combinational circuit computes, and the rule for reading one
steps.body: A combinational circuit has no memory: its output depends only on the present inputs. To find its function, write the output of each gate in terms of its inputs, working from the inputs towards the output. A NAND gives $\overline{PQ}$, a NOT gives $\overline{P}$, an AND gives $PQ$, an OR gives $P+Q$. Two expressions are the same function exactly when they agree on every input row, and for two variables there are only four rows.

steps.title: Read the three gates
steps.body: Gate 1 (NAND of $Y$ and $X$) gives $\overline{XY}$. Gate 2 (NOT of $X$) gives $\overline{X}$. Gate 3 (AND of $X$ with the inverted $Y$) gives $X\overline{Y}$. The OR combines them.

steps.title: Simplify
steps.body: By De Morgan, $\overline{XY}=\overline{X}+\overline{Y}$, so $F=\overline{X}+\overline{Y}+\overline{X}+X\overline{Y}$. The repeated $\overline{X}$ merges, leaving $F=\overline{X}+\overline{Y}+X\overline{Y}$. The term $X\overline{Y}$ is already inside $\overline{Y}$ (if $\overline{Y}=1$ then $X\overline{Y}$ adds nothing), so $F=\overline{X}+\overline{Y}=\overline{XY}$.

steps.title: Check each option on all four rows
steps.body: $F$ is 1 for $XY=00,01,10$ and 0 for $XY=11$. Option (A) $\overline{XY}$ is exactly that. Option (B) is $\overline{X}+\overline{Y}+X\overline{Y}=\overline{X}+\overline{Y}$, the same. Option (C) is the circuit expression itself. Option (D) $X+\overline{Y}$ gives 0 for $X=0,Y=1$ where $F=1$, so it is wrong. Correct: (A), (B), (C).

shortcut.body: Read the circuit straight off: $F=\overline{XY}+\overline{X}+X\overline{Y}$, which is option (C) with no work. Then note $\overline{XY}=\overline{X}+\overline{Y}$ already contains the other two terms, so $F=\overline{XY}$: (A), and (B) written out is the same sum. For (D) test one row, $X=0,Y=1$: $F=1$ but $X+\overline{Y}=0$. About one minute.

traps.text: Choosing (D) $X+\overline{Y}$ by mixing up which input is inverted. It differs from $F$ at $XY=01$ (and $11$ too, where it gives 1 while $F=0$).
Leaving out (A) because it does not look like the circuit: $\overline{XY}$ is the simplified form of the whole circuit, so it is correct. In an MSQ every equivalent form scores.
Leaving out (B) because of the extra $X\overline{Y}$ term. That term is redundant (absorbed by $\overline{Y}$), so (B) still equals $\overline{X}+\overline{Y}$.

recognize.clues: A circuit of three small gates (NAND, NOT, AND) feeds one OR gate, and the question asks which expressions equal the output $F$. This is reading a circuit and testing equivalence over a short truth table.
recognize.contrast: The NAND gate hints at universal-gate questions, but nothing here asks to build a gate from NAND gates. The task is to read the output function and compare forms, so use the truth table, not gate conversion.

check.body: Reason about when $F$ can be 0. An OR gate is 0 only when all three inputs are 0. The NAND output is 0 only at $X=Y=1$, and in that row the NOT of $X$ and the AND $X\overline{Y}$ are also 0. So $F$ is 0 in exactly the one row $X=Y=1$ and 1 in the other three, which is the truth table of a single NAND of $X$ and $Y$.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2025 Set 2, Question 21
GATE 2025 CS-2 final answer key, IIT Roorkee

hints.text: Two output functions are the same when they agree on every input row. With only X and Y, how many rows are there, and what does the circuit output on each?
A NAND gate gives the complement of the AND, a NOT gate flips its input, an AND gate needs both inputs at 1, and an OR gate is 1 when any input is 1.

Write each gate output as an expression in X and Y, OR the three together, and compare that function with each option, by truth table or by De Morgan and absorption. In an MSQ every option equal to F is correct.
Build a four-row truth table for XY = 00, 01, 10, 11 with one column per gate, one for F, and one column for each option. Then compare the columns row by row.
In the row X = 1, Y = 1 the NAND gives 0, the NOT gives 0 and the AND with inverted Y gives 0, so F is 0 there. Test the options on that row first, then on the rest.

variation.stem: A circuit has three gates feeding an OR gate with output $F$: a NOR gate of $X$ and $Y$, an AND gate of $X$ and $Y$, and an AND gate of $X$ with inverted $Y$. Which is/are the CORRECT option(s) for $F$?
options: $X + \overline{Y}$
$\overline{X}\,\overline{Y} + XY + X\overline{Y}$
$\overline{X} + Y$
$\overline{X}\,\overline{Y} + XY$
variation.explanation: The three gates give $\overline{X}\,\overline{Y}$, $XY$ and $X\overline{Y}$. Together $F=\overline{X}\,\overline{Y}+XY+X\overline{Y}$, and since $XY+X\overline{Y}=X$, this is $\overline{X}\,\overline{Y}+X=X+\overline{Y}$. Option C gives 0 at $X=1,Y=0$ where $F=1$, and option D, which leaves out the $X\overline{Y}$ term, also gives 0 there, so both fail.

questions.stem: Consider the circuit shown below where the gates may have propagation delays. Assume that all signal transitions occur instantaneously and that wires have no delays. Which of the following statements about the circuit is/are CORRECT?
questions.figure: Input X feeds one input of a two-input AND gate directly, and also feeds a NOT gate whose output is the other input of the AND gate. The AND output is Y.

diagram.alt: Input X goes straight to one input of an AND gate and through a NOT gate to the other input; the AND output is Y.

solutionDiagram.alt: Timing diagram of X, NOT X and Y: when X rises, Y pulses to 1 for one NOT delay; when X falls, Y stays 0.

options: With no propagation delays, the output $Y$ is always logic Zero
With no propagation delays, the output $Y$ is always logic One
With propagation delays, the output $Y$ can have a transient logic One after $X$ transitions from logic Zero to logic One
With propagation delays, the output $Y$ can have a transient logic Zero after $X$ transitions from logic One to logic Zero

steps.title: Terms: propagation delay and glitch
steps.body: A gate does not change its output at the instant its input changes: the output follows after a short time, the propagation delay. A glitch is a short unwanted pulse that appears at an output because two paths from the same input arrive at a gate at different times. A circuit with no delays shows only its Boolean function; a circuit with delays can also show glitches. Here $Y=X\cdot\overline{X}$.

steps.title: No delays
steps.body: Without delays, $X$ and $\overline{X}$ are always opposite, so $X\cdot\overline{X}=0$ for both values of $X$. $Y$ is always logic Zero: (A) is true and (B) is false.

steps.title: X rises from 0 to 1 with delays
steps.body: The direct path carries the new value 1 to the AND gate at once. The NOT gate takes one delay to turn its output from 1 to 0, so for that short time the AND gate sees $1$ and $1$ and outputs 1. Then the NOT output falls and $Y$ returns to 0. This is a transient One: (C) is true.

steps.title: X falls from 1 to 0 with delays
steps.body: The direct path drops to 0 at once, so the AND gate has a 0 input and $Y$ stays 0. The NOT output rises to 1 a delay later, but the other input is already 0. The output never leaves 0, and a transient Zero is meaningless when $Y$ was Zero already. (D) is false.

shortcut.body: $Y=X\overline{X}$ is 0 by algebra, so (A) true, (B) false. For the delay options ask which edge makes both AND inputs 1 together: a rising $X$ (the NOT output is still 1 for a moment). A falling $X$ makes the direct input 0 first, so no overlap. Answer A and C, about one minute.

traps.text: Taking $X+\overline{X}=1$ instead of $X\cdot\overline{X}=0$: the gate is an AND, not an OR.
Thinking a falling $X$ also glitches. The glitch needs both AND inputs to be 1 at once, and on a falling edge the direct input drops before the inverted input rises.
Dropping (C) because the answer "is zero" in algebra. The function is 0 in steady state; the glitch is only a timing effect, and that is exactly what (C) asks about.

recognize.clues: The stem says the gates may have propagation delays and asks about transient values after $X$ changes. The circuit feeds $X$ and its own complement into one AND gate, so the delay between the two paths is what matters.
recognize.contrast: A steady-state simplification question would stop at $X\cdot\overline{X}=0$, which settles only the no-delay options. The transient options need a timing view of the two paths, not Boolean algebra.

check.body: Boundary case: make the NOT gate instantaneous. Then the two AND inputs are never 1 together, no pulse can form, and $Y$ stays 0, which agrees with the no-delay statements. With a larger NOT delay the pulse after a rising edge simply lasts longer, so the width of the transient equals the NOT delay.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2024 Set 1, Question 18
GATE 2024 CS1 final answer key, IISc Bengaluru

hints.text: First ask what Y equals once all signals have settled. Then ask what could change if the two inputs of the AND gate do not change at the same instant.
A gate output lags its input by a small propagation delay, so the two copies of X reaching the AND gate, one direct and one through the NOT gate, can briefly disagree with their settled values.
An AND gate outputs 1 only while both inputs are 1, so look for a moment when the direct input and the inverted input are 1 together.
Draw a timeline for each edge of X. The direct wire changes at once and the NOT output changes one delay later. For each edge, write the two AND inputs during the gap between the two changes.
When X goes from 0 to 1, the direct input is already at its new value during the gap while the NOT output has not yet moved. Read the AND output in that gap, then repeat for the other edge.

variation.stem: Consider a circuit where the gates may have propagation delays, wires have none, and transitions are instantaneous. Input $X$ goes straight to one input of a two-input OR gate and also through a NOT gate to the other input; the OR output is $Y$. Which statements are CORRECT?
options: With no propagation delays, the output $Y$ is always logic One
With no propagation delays, the output $Y$ is always logic Zero
With propagation delays, the output $Y$ can have a transient logic Zero after $X$ goes from logic Zero to logic One
With propagation delays, the output $Y$ can have a transient logic Zero after $X$ goes from logic One to logic Zero
variation.explanation: With no delay $Y=X+\overline{X}=1$, so the first statement holds. On a falling edge the direct input drops to 0 at once while the NOT output is still 0 for one delay, so both OR inputs are 0 and $Y$ dips to 0. On a rising edge the direct input is already 1, so $Y$ never leaves 1.

questions.stem:
Consider a digital logic circuit consisting of three 2-to-1 multiplexers M1, M2, and M3 as shown below. X1 and X2 are inputs of M1. X3 and X4 are inputs of M2. A, B, and C are select lines of M1, M2, and M3, respectively.

For an instance of inputs $X1=1$, $X2=1$, $X3=0$, and $X4=0$, the number of combinations of A, B, C that give the output $Y=1$ is _________
questions.figure: M1 is a 2-to-1 multiplexer with data input 0 = X1, input 1 = X2, select A, output Q1. M2 is a 2-to-1 multiplexer with input 0 = X3, input 1 = X4, select B, output Q2. M3 is a 2-to-1 multiplexer with input 0 = Q1, input 1 = Q2, select C, output Y.

diagram.alt: Two 2-to-1 multiplexers M1 (inputs X1, X2, select A) and M2 (inputs X3, X4, select B) feed inputs 0 and 1 of multiplexer M3 with select C and output Y.

solutionDiagram.alt: The same circuit with Q1 always 1, Q2 always 0, and C selecting between them, so Y is 1 exactly when C is 0.

steps.title: What a 2-to-1 multiplexer does
steps.body: A 2-to-1 multiplexer (MUX) has two data inputs, numbered 0 and 1, one select line and one output. The rule: when the select is 0 the output equals data input 0, and when the select is 1 the output equals data input 1. The question counts combinations of the three select bits $A,B,C$ (8 in all) that make $Y=1$.

steps.title: Evaluate M1 and M2
steps.body: M1 picks $X1$ or $X2$, and both are 1, so $Q1=1$ whatever $A$ is. M2 picks $X3$ or $X4$, and both are 0, so $Q2=0$ whatever $B$ is.

steps.title: Evaluate M3
steps.body: M3 outputs $Q1$ when $C=0$ and $Q2$ when $C=1$. Thus $Y=1$ exactly when $C=0$, and $Y=0$ when $C=1$. In other words, $Y=\overline{C}$.

steps.title: Count
steps.body: $Y=1$ needs $C=0$. $A$ and $B$ are free, each with 2 values, so there are $2\times 2=4$ combinations $(A,B,C)$: 000, 010, 100, 110. The answer is 4.

shortcut.body: The data values are equal inside each first-level MUX (1,1 and 0,0), so $A$ and $B$ do not matter. Then $Y$ copies $Q1=1$ when $C=0$: half of the 8 combinations, which is 4. Safe because both inputs of each first-level MUX are equal.

traps.text: Answering 8 by thinking $Y=1$ for every combination because "two inputs are 1": M3 can also pass $Q2=0$.
Answering 2 by counting only $C=0$ and fixing $A$ and $B$, or 1 by counting only one combination. $A$ and $B$ are free, so each valid $C$ value yields 4 combinations in all.
Answering 3 or 6 by using a single-input match, such as counting combinations where either X1 or X2 is selected, instead of evaluating Q1 and Q2 first.

recognize.clues: The stem gives fixed data values $X1$ to $X4$ and three cascaded 2-to-1 multiplexers, then counts select combinations with $Y=1$. Evaluating the tree stage by stage with known data is the method.
recognize.contrast: This is not the multiplexer-as-function-generator task, where data inputs are chosen to realise a given Boolean function. Here the data are given and the selects are the unknowns being counted.

check.body: Test two rows directly. For $A=1,B=0,C=0$: M1 passes $X2=1$, M3 passes the M1 output, so $Y=1$. For $A=0,B=1,C=1$: M2 passes $X4=0$ and M3 passes the M2 output, so $Y=0$. Changing $A$ or $B$ in either row changes nothing, and flipping $C$ flips $Y$, so exactly the rows of one value of $C$ qualify.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2024 Set 1, Question 54
GATE 2024 CS1 final answer key, IISc Bengaluru

hints.text: Look at the data inputs of M1 and M2 before thinking about A, B and C. What do you notice about the two values each of them chooses between?
A 2-to-1 multiplexer copies its data input 0 when its select is 0 and its data input 1 when its select is 1.
If both data inputs of a multiplexer are equal, its select line has no effect on the output. Such a select line can take either value, so it doubles the count of combinations.
Find Q1 and Q2 first, then write Y in terms of the one select line that still matters. Count the values of that line that give Y=1 and multiply by the free choices of the other lines.
M1 passes a fixed value whatever A is. Work out M2 and M3 yourself.

variation.stem: Three 2-to-1 multiplexers are connected as follows. M1 has inputs $X1$ (input 0) and $X2$ (input 1) with select A. M2 has inputs $X3$ and $X4$ with select B. M3 has the output of M1 as input 0 and the output of M2 as input 1, with select C and output Y. For $X1=1$, $X2=0$, $X3=1$ and $X4=1$, how many combinations of A, B, C give $Y=1$?
variation.explanation: M2 has equal inputs, so $Q2=1$ for every $B$. M1 gives $Q1=1$ when $A=0$ and $Q1=0$ when $A=1$. For $C=1$, $Y=Q2=1$ for all 4 pairs of $A,B$. For $C=0$, $Y=Q1$ needs $A=0$, with $B$ free, giving 2 combinations. Total $4+2=6$.

questions.stem:
A Boolean digital circuit is composed using two 4-input multiplexers (M1 and M2) and one 2-input multiplexer (M3) as shown in the figure. X0-X7 are the inputs of the multiplexers M1 and M2 and could be connected to either 0 or 1. The select lines of the multiplexers are connected to Boolean variables A, B and C as shown.

Which one of the following set of values of (X0, X1, X2, X3, X4, X5, X6, X7) will realise the Boolean function $\overline{A} + \overline{A}\cdot\overline{C} + A\cdot\overline{B}\cdot C$?
questions.figure: M1 is a 4-input multiplexer with data inputs 0 to 3 connected to X0, X1, X2, X3; its select lines are S1 = A and S0 = C. M2 is a 4-input multiplexer with data inputs 0 to 3 connected to X4, X5, X6, X7; its select lines are S1 = A and S0 = C. M3 is a 2-input multiplexer with input 0 = output of M1, input 1 = output of M2, select S = B. The output of M3 is the circuit output.

diagram.alt: Two 4-input multiplexers M1 (X0 to X3) and M2 (X4 to X7), both selected by A as S1 and C as S0, feed inputs 0 and 1 of a 2-input multiplexer M3 selected by B.

solutionDiagram.alt: Truth table of the function over A, B, C showing which multiplexer M3 picks, which X input is read, and the required value; the values X0 to X7 are 1,1,0,1,1,1,0,0.

steps.title: How a multiplexer tree selects one input
steps.body: A 4-input multiplexer with select lines $S_1S_0$ passes data input number $2S_1+S_0$ to its output. A 2-input multiplexer with select $B$ passes input 0 when $B=0$ and input 1 when $B=1$. Putting constants 0 or 1 on the data inputs makes the whole tree a lookup table: each row of the truth table of $f(A,B,C)$ reads exactly one $X_i$, and that $X_i$ must hold the value of $f$ on that row.

steps.title: Which Xi each row reads
steps.body: $B$ decides the multiplexer: $B=0$ reads M1 (X0 to X3) and $B=1$ reads M2 (X4 to X7). Inside it, $S_1=A$ and $S_0=C$ pick input $2A+C$. So row $(A,B,C)$ reads $X_{4B+2A+C}$.

steps.title: Tabulate f
steps.body: $f=\overline{A}+\overline{A}\,\overline{C}+A\overline{B}C$. The second term is inside the first, so $f=\overline{A}+A\overline{B}C$. For $A=0$, $f=1$. For $A=1$, $f=1$ only when $B=0,C=1$. Rows: $X_0$ (000)=1, $X_1$ (001)=1, $X_2$ (100)=0, $X_3$ (101)=1, $X_4$ (010)=1, $X_5$ (011)=1, $X_6$ (110)=0, $X_7$ (111)=0.

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: The vector $(1,1,0,1,1,1,0,0)$ is option (C). Options (A), (B) and (D) each differ in at least one position, for example (A) has $X_3=0$ though $A=1,B=0,C=1$ must give 1.

shortcut.body: $f=\overline{A}+A\overline{B}C$ has zeros only when $A=1$ and not ($B=0$, $C=1$): rows 100, 110, 111, which read $X_2,X_6,X_7$. So the vector is 0 exactly at positions 2, 6 and 7, option (C). Check only those three positions across the options.

traps.text: Setting $X_3=0$ and $X_6=1$: indexing the rows as $4C+2A+B$, so that $C$ drives the select of M3 and $B$ becomes the low select bit of M1 and M2. The row $A=1,B=0,C=1$ then lands on $X_6$ and the row $A=1,B=1,C=0$ on $X_3$, which is not how the figure is wired.
Putting the lone 1 of the $A=1$ side in $X_7$ rather than $X_3$: that reads $A=1,B=1,C=1$ instead of $A=1,B=0,C=1$, confusing which multiplexer $B=1$ selects.
(D) puts 0 on $X_0$ and $X_1$, which are the rows $A=0,B=0$. The term $\overline{A}$ forces $f=1$ there, so it fails at once.

recognize.clues: The options are vectors of constants for the data inputs of a multiplexer tree and the stem gives a Boolean function to realise. The function is given and the data inputs are the unknowns.
recognize.contrast: In a plain multiplexer evaluation the data are known and the selects are chosen. Here it is the reverse, so build the truth table of the function and read it into the data inputs by the wiring index.

check.body: Test two rows of the function against the vector. For $A=1,B=0,C=1$ the function is $0+0+1=1$ and the wiring reads $X_3$, which must be 1. For $A=1,B=1,C=0$ the function is 0 and the wiring reads $X_6$, which must be 0. A vector with $X_3=0$ or $X_6=1$ is therefore impossible.

sources.label: GATE 2023 CS answer key, IIT Kanpur

hints.text: Think of the circuit as a lookup table: each of the 8 rows of (A, B, C) reads exactly one of X0 to X7. What do you need to know about the function, and what about the wiring?
A 4-input multiplexer with selects S1 and S0 passes data input number 2·S1 + S0, and a 2-input multiplexer passes input 0 or input 1 according to its select.
The data input that a row reads must hold the value of the function on that row. So the vector of X values is the truth table of the function, listed in the order the wiring produces.
Simplify the function first by absorption. Then use the figure to find which Xi each (A, B, C) row reads, and write the function value row by row in order X0 to X7.
The term $\overline{A}\,\overline{C}$ lies inside $\overline{A}$, so the function reduces to $\overline{A}+A\overline{B}C$. Every row with A=0 gives 1, which fixes four entries of the vector.

variation.stem: A circuit has two 4-input multiplexers M1 (data inputs X0 to X3) and M2 (data inputs X4 to X7), both with S1 = A and S0 = C, and a 2-input multiplexer M3 with input 0 from M1, input 1 from M2 and select B. Each Xi is wired to 0 or 1. Which vector $(X0,\dots,X7)$ realises $\overline{A}B+A\overline{C}$?
variation.explanation: Row $(A,B,C)$ reads $X_{4B+2A+C}$. The function $\overline{A}B+A\overline{C}$ is 1 when $A=0,B=1$ or when $A=1,C=0$, and 0 otherwise. Listing it by index gives (0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0). Option A uses the index $4C+2A+B$, option C uses $4A+2B+C$, and option D is the complement.

questions.stem: Consider a digital display system (DDS) shown in the figure that displays the contents of register X. A 16-bit code word is used to load a word in X, either from S or from R. S is a 1024-word memory segment and R is a 32-word register file. Based on the value of mode bit M, T selects an input word to load in X. P and Q interface with the corresponding bits in the code word to choose the addressed word. Which one of the following represents the functionality of P, Q, and T?
questions.figure: The 16-bit code word has three fields: mode bit M, S-address and R-address. The S-address field goes into block P, whose output goes to S. The R-address field goes into block Q, whose output goes to R. The outputs of S and R both go into block T. The mode bit M also goes into T. The output of T is loaded into register X, which feeds the DDS display.

diagram.alt: Code word split into M, S-address and R-address; S-address goes through P to memory S, R-address through Q to register file R; S, R and M feed T, whose output goes to register X and the DDS.

solutionDiagram.alt: The same block diagram with P labelled a 10 to 1024 decoder, Q a 5 to 32 decoder and T a 2 to 1 multiplexer, and the code word bit count 1 plus 10 plus 5 equal to 16.

options: P is 10:1 multiplexer; Q is 5:1 multiplexer; T is 2:1 multiplexer
P is 10:$2^{10}$ decoder; Q is 5:$2^5$ decoder; T is 2:1 encoder
P is 10:$2^{10}$ decoder; Q is 5:$2^5$ decoder; T is 2:1 multiplexer
P is 1:10 de-multiplexer; Q is 1:5 de-multiplexer; T is 2:1 multiplexer

steps.title: The four building blocks and what each is for
steps.body: A decoder with $n$ input bits has $2^n$ output lines and turns on exactly one of them, the one whose number is the input value; it is how an address selects one word. A multiplexer (MUX) selects one of several data inputs and sends it to a single output, using select bits. A demultiplexer does the reverse: one data input goes to one of several outputs. An encoder turns a one-hot input into its binary number and cannot select between two data words. The rule for the question: use the block whose job matches "address picks a word" and "one bit chooses between two words".

steps.title: Size P and Q from the word counts
steps.body: S has 1024 words, so an address needs $\log_2 1024=10$ bits, and P must be a decoder with 10 inputs and $2^{10}$ outputs (one word line per word). R has 32 words, so $\log_2 32=5$ bits and Q is a 5 to $2^5$ decoder. The code word then has $1+10+5=16$ bits, which agrees with the stem.

steps.title: Choose T
steps.body: T receives one word from S and one word from R and passes exactly one of them, chosen by the single bit M. That is a 2:1 multiplexer. An encoder would do something else (convert a one-hot code to binary), so it cannot be T.

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: P: 10 to $2^{10}$ decoder, Q: 5 to $2^5$ decoder, T: 2:1 multiplexer is option (C). A multiplexer for P or Q (A) would take 10 or 5 data inputs, not an address, and (D) uses de-multiplexers that need a data input, not an address.

shortcut.body: Say it in words: "address picks a word" is a decoder (rules out A and D), and "one bit chooses between two words" is a multiplexer, not an encoder (rules out B). Option (C) in under a minute, with no calculation beyond $2^{10}=1024$ and $2^5=32$.

traps.text: Using multiplexers for P and Q: a 10:1 multiplexer has only 10 data inputs and could not address 1024 words. Multiplexers select data, not memory words from an address.
Choosing an encoder for T. An encoder makes a binary code from a one-hot input; it cannot choose between the S word and the R word.
Using 1:10 and 1:5 de-multiplexers: those have the wrong shape. They would send one data bit to one of 10 or 5 outputs, whereas the address has 10 and 5 bits and must select among 1024 and 32 lines.

recognize.clues: A memory of 1024 words is addressed by one field, a register file of 32 words by another, and a single mode bit chooses between the two words read. Address fields feeding word lines point to decoders.
recognize.contrast: A multiplexer also appears in this circuit (block T), so tell them apart by the data flow: a decoder takes an address and produces word-select lines, while a multiplexer takes data words and produces one data output.

check.body: Test the word count: a decoder with 10 inputs has 1024 outputs, one per word of S, whereas a multiplexer with 10 data inputs could reach only 10 words. That rules out a multiplexer for P.

sources.label: GATE 2022 CS answer key, IIT Kharagpur

hints.text: For each of P, Q and T ask what job it does: picking one word out of a memory by an address, or choosing one of two words by a mode bit. Which kind of block does each job?
A decoder turns an n-bit number into one active line among $2^n$, a multiplexer chooses one of several data inputs, and an encoder goes the other way, from one active line to a number.

An address field of n bits can name one of $2^n$ words. Ask how many separate lines a block needs so that every word of its memory can be reached, and what a block needs to pass just one of two words.
Take the number of words in S and in R, turn each into a bit count with log base 2, and compare with the field widths in the 16-bit code word. Then decide the type of each block from its job.
S holds 1024 words and $2^{10}=1024$, so the S-address field has 10 bits and P has 10 input lines. Do the same for R with its 32 words.

variation.stem: A display system loads register X from either S, a memory segment of 2048 words, or R, a register file of 64 words, using an 18-bit code word that holds a mode bit M, the S-address and the R-address. Block P takes the S-address, block Q takes the R-address, and block T selects the word to load into X based on M. Which one of the following represents the functionality of P, Q and T?
options: P is 11:1 multiplexer; Q is 6:1 multiplexer; T is 2:1 multiplexer
P is 11:$2^{11}$ decoder; Q is 6:$2^{6}$ decoder; T is 2:1 multiplexer
P is 11:$2^{11}$ decoder; Q is 6:$2^{6}$ decoder; T is 2:1 encoder
P is $2^{11}$:11 encoder; Q is $2^{6}$:6 encoder; T is 2:1 multiplexer
variation.explanation: $\log_2 2048=11$ and $\log_2 64=6$, so with the mode bit the code word has $1+11+6=18$ bits. An address field that selects one word is handled by a decoder, so P is 11 to $2^{11}$ and Q is 6 to $2^6$. T chooses between two words with one bit, which is a 2:1 multiplexer.

questions.stem:
Which one of the following circuits implements the Boolean function given below?

$f(x,y,z)=m_0+m_1+m_3+m_4+m_5+m_6$, where $m_i$ is the $i^{th}$ minterm.
questions.figure: Four circuits, each a 4x1 multiplexer with select lines s1 = y and s0 = z, output f, and data inputs 0, 1, 2, 3 as follows. (A) 1, 1, x, x'. (B) x, 1, x', 1. (C) 1, 1, x', x. (D) x', 1, x, 1.

diagram.alt: Four 4x1 multiplexers with select lines y and z. Option A has inputs 1, 1, x, x-prime; B has x, 1, x-prime, 1; C has 1, 1, x-prime, x; D has x-prime, 1, x, 1.

solutionDiagram.alt: Table of each y z value with its minterm pair, the value of f at x equal 0 and 1, and the data input required: 1, 1, x, x-prime, matching option A.

options: Inputs 0 to 3 of the multiplexer: 1, 1, $x$, $x'$
Inputs 0 to 3 of the multiplexer: $x$, 1, $x'$, 1
Inputs 0 to 3 of the multiplexer: 1, 1, $x'$, $x$
Inputs 0 to 3 of the multiplexer: $x'$, 1, $x$, 1

steps.title: Minterms and how a multiplexer builds a function
steps.body: The minterm $m_i$ of $f(x,y,z)$ is the input row whose binary number $xyz$ equals $i$, with $x$ the high bit. A function equals the OR of the minterms where it is 1. A 4x1 multiplexer with selects $s_1=y$, $s_0=z$ passes data input number $2y+z$. To implement $f$, give each value of $yz$ the data input that equals $f$ as a function of the one remaining variable $x$ (Shannon expansion on $y,z$).

steps.title: Group the minterms by yz
steps.body: For $yz=00$ the rows are $m_0$ ($x=0$) and $m_4$ ($x=1$); both are in $f$, so $f=1$. For $yz=01$: $m_1$ and $m_5$, both in $f$, so $f=1$. For $yz=10$: $m_2$ (not in $f$) and $m_6$ (in $f$), so $f=x$. For $yz=11$: $m_3$ (in $f$) and $m_7$ (not in $f$), so $f=\overline{x}$.

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: The required data inputs are $1,1,x,\overline{x}$, which is option (A). Options (B) and (D) put $x$ or $\overline{x}$ on input 0, which would make $f(0,0,0)$ or $f(1,0,0)$ equal 0, but both $m_0$ and $m_4$ are in $f$. Option (C) swaps $x$ and $\overline{x}$ on inputs 2 and 3.

shortcut.body: Only two minterms are missing: $m_2$ and $m_7$. The pairs $yz=00$ and $01$ have both minterms, so inputs 0 and 1 are 1: only (A) and (C) remain. Then $yz=10$ has $m_6$ ($x=1$) only, so input 2 is $x$: (A). About one minute.

traps.text: Swapping $x$ and $\overline{x}$ on inputs 2 and 3: for $yz=10$ the surviving minterm is $m_6$ where $x=1$, so the input is $x$, not $\overline{x}$.
Putting $x$ on input 0: both $m_0$ and $m_4$ are in $f$, so that input must be the constant 1, not $x$.

Writing $\overline{x}$ on input 0 and 1 on input 3 without checking $m_4$ and $m_7$: $m_4$ is in $f$ but is lost when input 0 is $\overline{x}$, and $m_7$ is not in $f$ but is added when input 3 is 1.

recognize.clues: The function is given as a sum of minterms of $x,y,z$ and each option is a 4x1 multiplexer whose selects are $y$ and $z$ and whose data inputs are constants or $x$ and its complement. That is the setup of a function realised by Shannon expansion.
recognize.contrast: A decoder with an OR gate can also build a minterm sum, but the options here are all multiplexers. With selects y and z, the data inputs must be functions of the one leftover variable x.

check.body: Test one minterm in and one out for the two inputs that depend on $x$. $m_6$ ($x=1,y=1,z=0$) is in $f$ and input 2 of option A is $x=1$, giving 1. $m_2$ ($x=0$) is not in $f$ and input 2 is $x=0$. $m_3$ ($x=0,y=z=1$) is in $f$ and input 3 is $\overline{x}=1$. $m_7$ is not in $f$ and input 3 is $\overline{x}=0$.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2021 Set 2, Question 5
GATE 2021 CS-2 answer key, IIT Bombay

hints.text: The select lines are y and z, so each data input can depend only on x. For each pair of values of y and z, which two minterms are involved, and what does f do as x changes?
A multiplexer with selects y and z passes data input number 2y + z. A minterm $m_i$ is the truth-table row whose xyz, read as a binary number with x as the high bit, equals i.
For a fixed yz, f as a function of x can only be 0 for both values, 1 for both values, equal to x, or equal to the complement of x. Those four are the only possible data input values.
For each of the four yz pairs, list its two minterm numbers (x=0 gives $m_{yz}$ and x=1 gives $m_{4+yz}$) and mark which of them appear in the given sum.
For yz = 00 the minterms are $m_0$ and $m_4$, and both appear in f, so input 0 does not depend on x. Do the other three pairs the same way.

variation.stem: Which one of the following circuits implements $f(x,y,z)=m_0+m_1+m_2+m_5+m_7$, where $m_i$ is the $i^{th}$ minterm? Each circuit is a 4x1 multiplexer with select lines $s_1=y$ and $s_0=z$, and the options list data inputs 0 to 3.
options: Inputs 0 to 3 of the multiplexer: $x$, 1, $x$, $x'$
Inputs 0 to 3 of the multiplexer: $x'$, 1, $x'$, $x$
Inputs 0 to 3 of the multiplexer: $x'$, 1, $x$, $x'$
Inputs 0 to 3 of the multiplexer: $x'$, 1, $x'$, 1
variation.explanation: Group by $yz$. For $yz=00$ the minterms are $m_0$ (in) and $m_4$ (out), so the input is $x'$. For $01$: $m_1$ and $m_5$ are both in, so 1. For $10$: $m_2$ in and $m_6$ out, so $x'$. For $11$: $m_3$ out and $m_7$ in, so $x$. The inputs are $x',1,x',x$.

questions.stem: A multiplexer is placed between a group of 32 registers and an accumulator to regulate data movement such that at any given point in time the content of only one register will move to the accumulator. The minimum number of select lines needed for the multiplexer is ___________.

steps.title: What select lines do
steps.body: A multiplexer (MUX) with $N$ data inputs sends exactly one of them to its output. Which one is decided by the select lines, which carry a binary number. With $s$ select lines there are $2^s$ different binary numbers, so a MUX can choose among at most $2^s$ inputs. The rule is $N\le 2^s$, so the minimum is $s=\lceil\log_2 N\rceil$.

steps.title: Apply to 32 registers
steps.body: Each of the 32 registers is one data input, and only one at a time moves to the accumulator, so $N=32$. Four select lines give $2^4=16<32$, which is too few. Five give $2^5=32$, exactly enough.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The minimum number of select lines is 5, matching the official key.

shortcut.body: Count the bits needed to number 32 things: $32=2^5$, so 5. If $N$ is not a power of 2, round up (for instance 33 inputs need 6). Ten seconds.

traps.text: Answering 32 (one select line per register): that is a one-hot scheme. A MUX reads a binary number, so far fewer lines are needed.
Answering 4 by using $\log_2(32)-1$ or by counting $2^4=16$ pairs; 4 lines can select only 16 registers.
Answering 6 by counting the 5 bits of the register number plus one for the accumulator. The accumulator is the output, not an input to select.

recognize.clues: A multiplexer sits between a group of 32 registers and one accumulator, and only one register moves at a time. The question asks for the minimum number of select lines, which depends only on the number of data inputs.
recognize.contrast: A decoder with 32 outputs needs the same count of input lines but produces one active line per register. Here the multiplexer collapses 32 data inputs to one output, so the register count sets the select lines.

check.body: Boundary check. With 5 lines the codes 00000 to 11111 give exactly 32 distinct names, so every register is reachable and no code is spare. Removing one register (31) would still need 5 lines, since 4 lines name only 16, and the count would fall to 4 lines only at 16 registers.

sources.label: GATE 2020 CS answer key, IIT Delhi

hints.text: Think of the select lines as a binary number that names one register. How many different names are needed, and how many names can a given number of lines make?
A group of s binary lines can represent $2^s$ different values.
The select lines must be able to name every data input, so $2^s$ must be at least the number of data inputs. The minimum is the smallest s that satisfies this.
Write the number of registers as a power of 2, or find the smallest s with $2^s$ not below it. Only the data inputs are counted: the accumulator is the output of the multiplexer.
Check what 4 select lines can do: they name only 16 registers. Decide how many more lines are needed to name all of them.

variation.stem: A bus is fed by a bank of 48 input channels through a single multiplexer, and exactly one channel is connected to the bus at any moment. The minimum number of select lines the multiplexer needs is ___________.
variation.explanation: With $s$ select lines a multiplexer can choose among at most $2^s$ inputs. Here $2^5=32<48$ is too few and $2^6=64\ge 48$ is enough, so $s=\lceil\log_2 48\rceil=6$. The non-power-of-two count rounds up.

questions.stem: If there are $m$ input lines and $n$ output lines for a decoder that is used to uniquely address a byte addressable 1 KB RAM, then the minimum value of $m + n$ is ____ .

steps.title: What a decoder does
steps.body: A decoder with $m$ input lines has $n=2^m$ output lines. At any time the inputs form a binary number, and exactly one output line, the one with that number, is 1. In a RAM the decoder turns an address into a single word-select line. So to address $W$ locations uniquely, the decoder needs $2^m\ge W$ outputs.

steps.title: Count the locations
steps.body: The RAM is byte addressable and is 1 KB, so it has $1024=2^{10}$ bytes, each a separate location with its own address. The minimum is $m=10$ input lines, giving $n=2^{10}=1024$ output lines.

steps.title: Add
steps.body: $m+n=10+1024=1034$. Smaller $m$ gives fewer than 1024 outputs and cannot reach every byte. The answer is 1034.

shortcut.body: 1 KB = $2^{10}$ bytes, so the decoder is 10 to 1024: $10+1024=1034$. Do not forget to add the outputs.

traps.text: Answering 10 (only the address bits) or 1024 (only the outputs): the question asks for $m+n$.
Answering 1032 or 1033 by using 8 or 9 address lines, or 1024+8 for the byte width. The decoder addresses locations, not bits within a byte.
Using 1000 for 1 KB. In memory sizing a kilobyte is 1024 bytes.

recognize.clues: The stem gives a decoder with $m$ input lines and $n$ output lines used to address a byte addressable 1 KB RAM, and asks for the minimum $m+n$. One output line per byte is the clue.
recognize.contrast: An encoder does the reverse, many input lines to a binary code. Here the binary address goes in and one line out of $2^m$ comes active, so it is a decoder.

check.body: Test the neighbours. With $m=9$ the decoder has $2^9=512$ outputs, so only half of the 1024 bytes can be selected. With $m=11$ it has 2048 outputs, more than needed, so 10 is the least that works. At $m=10$ the outputs match the byte count exactly, giving a decoder with 1024 outputs and 10 inputs.

sources.label: GATE 2020 CS answer key, IIT Delhi

hints.text: What must the decoder be able to select, and how many separate things is that? Count them before thinking about wires.
A decoder turns a binary number on its input lines into a single active output line, so each output line stands for one input value.
With $m$ input lines there are $2^m$ distinct input patterns, so there are $2^m$ output lines. Unique addressing needs at least one output per addressable location.
Write the RAM size in bytes as a power of 2. Each byte has its own address, so that power is the number of address lines, and the decoder's output count follows from it.
The RAM size is $1\,\text{KB}=2^{10}$ bytes in memory sizing, not 1000. Find $m$ and $n$ from this, then form the sum the question asks for.

variation.stem: A decoder with $m$ input lines and $n$ output lines selects exactly one byte of a byte addressable ROM of size 2 KB, one output line per byte. Find the minimum value of $m + n$ (answer in integer).
variation.explanation: A 2 KB byte addressable RAM has $2048=2^{11}$ locations, so the decoder needs $m=11$ input lines and $n=2^{11}=2048$ output lines. The sum is $11+2048=2059$.
